top_choice_rationale: P002 (B030: Autor, Hanson, Dorn) is my narrow first choice on the common test of whether the work changed what can credibly be known and has been validated since. Newly assembled data and exposure-based quasi-experimental designs showed that import competition and technological change produce persistent, uneven local labour-market adjustment, and other authors have reproduced the core finding with different designs and in other countries. The citation is limited to the empirical labour-demand evidence, so credit rests on the identifiable Autor-Dorn-Hanson contribution and does not claim the wider task framework. I place it only slightly above P001 (B005: Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn). B005 is more mature and has a cleaner credit core, and I would be comfortable with it. The gap is a weighting judgement: I give somewhat more weight to a substantive, design-based finding about who bears the costs of technological and trade change than to a measurement toolkit. B030's weak points are the unsettled persistence and magnitude of the China-shock effects, the shift-share identification debate, and whether the trade and technology strands form one achievement. I weigh those and still keep it first, narrowly. I have not independently verified the claims about prior prizes or replication records. P000 is last because at least two mature, well-attributed candidates meet the bar.
recusal_note: No co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Hanson, Dorn, Pakes, Berry or Levinsohn is apparent from the profile. My field, labour economics, is close to B030, which may bias me toward it. I presented the 2023 Goldin prize, which is topically adjacent to B030; that presentation was an Academy text and not evidence of my preferences. I disclose these ties and do not adjudicate them.
